(p-70) Surah al-Insan is Madani, and its verses number thirty-one.

﴿Has there come upon man﴾: this is an interrogative (istifham) of affirmation and bringing near (taqrir wa taqrib), for "hal" here means "qad," and the original form is "a-hal atā" (Has there not come upon man...).

﴿upon man﴾: before a near time, ﴿a span of time﴾, that is, a limited portion existing from extended time.

﴿he was not a thing worth mentioning﴾, but rather he was a thing forgotten and not mentioned at all as human, such as the element (al-'unsur) and the drop (al-nutfah) and other than these. The negated clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "man," meaning "not worth mentioning," or it is another attribute of "a span" with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning "he was not in it a thing worth mentioning." The intended meaning of "man" is the species (al-jins). Thus the explicit noun in the Exalted saying:

Indeed, We created man from a drop of sperm-fluid. [The pronoun "We" is used] for emphasis (li-ziyadat al-taqrir). Or "man" refers to Adam, peace be upon him. This is what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Thawri, 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi. Ibn 'Abbas said, in the narration of Abu Salih from him: "Forty years passed over him before the spirit was breathed into him, and he was lying between Makkah and al-Ta'if." In the narration of al-Dahhak from him: "He was created from clay and remained for forty years; then from black, moulded clay (hama masnun) and remained for forty years; then from dry clay that rings (salsal) and remained for forty years. His creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years, and then the spirit was breathed into him." Al-Mawardi relayed from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the "hin" mentioned here is a long, extended period whose duration is known. In that case the first (﴿hin﴾) refers to the creation of his (Adam's) own person, peace and blessings be upon him, and this [statement] explains the creation of his descendants.

﴿Amshaj﴾ (mixtures): the plural of mishj or mashij, from "mashajtu al-shay'" when I created the thing. It describes the sperm-drop because what is meant by it is the combination of the two waters (male and female), and each of them has differing attributes of colour, thinness and thickness, and distinct properties. The man's water is white and thick, containing the power of coagulation, while the woman's water is yellow and thin, containing the power of formation (al-in'iqad). From the two the child is formed. Whatever is of sinew, bone and strength comes from the man's water, and whatever is of flesh, blood and hair comes from the woman's water. Al-Qurtubi said: this has been related as a hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said that the word is singular, like "a'shar" and "akyash". It was also said that "amshaj" means colours and stages, for the sperm-drop turns into a clot ('alaqah), then into a lump of flesh (mudghah), until the creation is complete.

The words of the Most High, ﴿nabtalihi﴾ (We try him), are a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "khalaqna" (We created), meaning: intending to test him with the obligations (taklif) that will come later; or conveying him from state to state by way of metaphor (isti'arah), as has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "We turn him in his mother's womb, a sperm-drop, then a clot, and so on to the end."

﴿So We made him hearing and seeing﴾: so that he may be able to listen to the revealed verses (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah) and observe the verses of creation (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah). Thus it is like something caused by the beginning [of creation]. For this reason it is joined by "fa" (then/so) to the creation, which is conditioned by it, and the Most High's words are arranged upon it:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ by sending down the verses and setting up the proofs.

﴿Either grateful or ungrateful﴾: these are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl, a grammatical state) referring back to the object of "guided" (hadaynā). That is, We enabled him and empowered him to follow the path that leads to the goal in both of his states. Or the particle "imma" is used for detailing (tafṣīl) or dividing (taqsīm), meaning: We guided him to that which leads to it in both of his states, or with him divided into two groups, some of them being grateful through being guided and taking up the way, and some of them being ungrateful through turning away from it. It has also been said that "the way" (al-sabīl) is what is meant here, i.e., We made him know the way, either as a grateful way or as an ungrateful way, by describing the way with the attribute of its traveller, metaphorically. It has been read as "ammā" with a fatḥah, on the basis of an omitted response (ḥadhf al-jawāb), meaning: as for the grateful, it is by Our enabling; and as for the ungrateful, it is by his own bad choice, not by mere compulsion from Us without any choice on his part. The mention of "the ungrateful" (al-kafūr) is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawāṣil) and to indicate that a human being rarely is free from some ingratitude, and that what he is held accountable for is excessive ingratitude (al-kufr al-mufraṭ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers﴾ from among the individuals of mankind who were guided to the path (al-sabil).

﴿Chains﴾ by which they are led.

﴿And shackles﴾ by which they are bound. ﴿And a blazing fire﴾ by which they are burned. The mention of their threat (wa'id) is placed first, although it comes later in order, so that the two may be joined in mention, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turned black...﴾ and so on. Also, because warning (indhar) is more important and more beneficial, and it is better to open and close the discourse with mention of the believers. Moreover, in their description there is a detail which, if placed earlier, might disturb the coherence (tajawub) of the parts of the noble composition. It is also read as (salasila) [in the accusative indefinite], for the sake of harmony (tanasub).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar)﴾ This begins an account of the good state of the grateful, following the account of the evil state of the disbelievers, and their being introduced under the title of righteousness (al-birr) serves to indicate the reason for which they deserved the noble honour they attained. Al-abrar is the plural of barr, or of barr (bārr), like "rabb" and "arbab" and "shahid" and "ashhad." It has been said: it is one who is dutiful (yabarru) to his Creator, i.e., obeys Him. It has been said: one who complies with the command of God, exalted is He. It has been said: one who fulfils the right of God, exalted is He, and fulfils vows. And from al-Hasan: the righteous (al-barr) is one who does not harm even an ant.

﴿They drink from a cup﴾ The cup (al-zujaja) is the glass when there is wine in it, and it is also applied to the wine itself. So "min" (from) is for the beginning of the source according to the first sense, and partitive or explicative according to the second.

﴿Whose mixture is﴾ i.e., that with which it is mixed, ﴿camphor﴾ i.e., water of camphor. It is the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is in the whiteness of camphor, its fragrance and its coolness. The sentence is an attribute of "cup." And the saying of the Exalted:

"Aynan" (a spring) is a substitute (badal) for "kafuran" (camphor). Qatadah said: it is mixed for them with camphor and sealed for them with musk. It was also said: its scent, whiteness and coolness are created for them, so it is as though it had been mixed with camphor. On these two views, "aynan" is a substitute (badal) for the place (mahall) of "min ka'sin" (from a cup), with an elided noun understood: they drink wine of a spring's wine (khamran khamra ayn), or it is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas).

The phrase ﴿the servants of Allah drink from it﴾ is an attributive description (sifah) of "aynan," meaning: they drink the wine with it, because it is mixed with it. It was also said that "yashrabu" (drink) is used in the sense of "yaltadhdhu" (take pleasure in), and it was said that the "ba'" (with) means "min" (from), and it was said that it is superfluous (za'idah). What supports this is the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah: "yashrabuha 'ibadu Allah" (the servants of Allah drink it). It was also said that the pronoun refers to the cup, and the meaning is: they drink the spring with that cup.

﴿they cause it to gush forth abundantly﴾: that is, they make it flow wherever they wish from their dwellings, an easy flow that is not withheld from them, but flows with force and rushing. The sentence is another attributive description (sifah) of "aynan." And the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 7:

﴿They fulfill their vows﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to explain the reason for which they were granted the bounties mentioned, and it contains a kind of detailing of what the name "the righteous" (al-abrar) indicates in summary. It is as if it were said: "What do they do so that they attain that lofty rank?" So it is said: "They fulfill what they have made obligatory upon themselves, so how about what Allah the Exalted has made obligatory upon them?" ﴿And they fear a day whose evil will be widespread﴾, its punishment, ﴿spreading far and wide﴾, spread out and dispersed throughout the regions to the utmost extent of dispersion, from "istatara al-harIq wal-fajr" (the fire and the dawn spread out). It is more emphatic than "tara" (flew), in the same relation as "istanfara" (to mobilize) is to "nafara" (to set out).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 8:

﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it﴾ That is: while they are themselves fond of food and in need of it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾. Or: out of love for giving food, so that it is done with a good disposition of the soul. Or: while they love Allah, exalted is He. Or: giving food that is rooted in His love, exalted is He, and this is the most fitting reading in light of what follows in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for the sake of Allah: the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾. "Captive" here means any captive: for the Prophet, peace be upon him, used to be brought a captive, and he would hand him over to one of the Muslims, saying: "Be good to him." Or it means a captive who is a believer, so that it includes the enslaved person and the imprisoned person. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ also called the debtor a captive, saying: ﴿Your debtor is your captive, so be good to your captive﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 9:**

﴿Indeed, we feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance﴾. This is on the presumption of a statement which occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "yut'imūn" (they feed), meaning: saying that, by the tongue of circumstance (lisān al-ḥāl), or by the tongue of speech (lisān al-maqāl), in order to remove the suspicion of reproach (mann), which nullifies charity, and the expectation of recompense, which diminishes the reward. And it is related from al-Ṣiddīqa (may Allah be pleased with her) that she used to send charity to a household, then she would ask the Messenger (ﷺ) what they had said. When he mentioned their supplication for them, she would supplicate for them with the like of it, so that the reward of the charity would remain purely hers with Allah, exalted is He.

﴿We do not want from you any recompense or thanks﴾. That is, "thanks" (shukr). This is a confirmation and emphasis of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a Day﴾, that is: the punishment of a day.

﴿Stern﴾: one in which faces will be made to frown, or [a day that] resembles a frowning lion in its severity and ferocity.

﴿Distressing﴾: intensely frowning. Therefore we do for you what we do, hoping that our Lord will save us by that from its evil. It has also been said that this is a justification for not desiring recompense or thanks, meaning: we fear the punishment of God Most High if we were to desire them.

"So Allah protected them from the evil of that Day" because of their fear and their guarding themselves against it. "And gave them radiance and joy": that is, He bestowed upon them, in place of the scowling and grief of the wicked, radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts.

(p-73) ﴿And He will reward them for their patience with a garden and silk﴾: for their patience in the hardships of acts of obedience, and in striving against the desires of the soul by abstaining from what is forbidden and by preferring others over wealth.

﴿A garden﴾: an orchard from which they eat whatever they wish. ﴿And silk﴾: which they wear and with which they adorn themselves.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that: "al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with both of them, fell ill, and the Prophet ﷺ visited them along with some people who were with him. They said to ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: 'If only you would make a vow concerning your son.' So ʿAli, Fatimah, and Fiddah—their female servant—may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them all, vowed that if they were cured of what they had, they would fast three days. Then they were cured, and they had nothing with them. So ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, borrowed three ṣāʿs of barley from Shamʿun al-Khaybari. Fatimah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, ground one ṣāʿ and baked five loaves, one for each of them, and they placed them before themselves to break their fast. A beggar stood over them and said: 'Peace be upon you, people of the house of Muhammad. A poor man from the poor of the Muslims; feed me, and Allah the Exalted will feed you from the banquets of Paradise.' So they gave him preference and spent the night having tasted nothing but water, and they awoke fasting. When evening came and they placed the food before themselves, an orphan stood over them, and they gave him preference. Then on the third day a captive stood over them, and they did the same. When morning came, ʿAli took the hands of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, and they came to the Prophet ﷺ. When he saw them trembling like chicks from the intensity of hunger, the Prophet, upon whom be prayers and peace, said: 'How greatly it grieves me to see you in this state.' He stood and went along with them, and he saw Fatimah in her prayer niche, her back pressed to her belly and her eyes sunken. That distressed him. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: 'Take it, O Muhammad; may Allah the Exalted bless you in your household.' Then he recited the surah to him."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 13:

﴿Reclining therein upon couches﴾. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun "them" in "He has rewarded them" (jaza-hum), and the governing element within it is "jaza" (rewarded). It has also been said that it is a qualifier (sifah) of "Paradise" (jannah), with the pronoun not being made explicit. "Al-ara'ik" (couches) are the thrones (surur) within canopied alcoves (hijal). The statement of the Exalted: ﴿They will see therein neither sun nor bitter cold﴾ is either a second circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun, or to the concealed pronoun in "reclining" (muttaki'in). The meaning is that a temperate air passes over them, neither scorching hot nor harmfully cold. It has also been said: "al-zamharir" means the moon in the dialect of the tribe of Tayy, and the meaning is that its air flows on its own, without needing a sun or a moon.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 14:

﴿And its shades drawing near over them﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to what precedes it, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) like it, or as a qualifier (ṣifa) of an omitted noun conjoined to "a garden" (jannah). And what other garden is it whose shades draw near over them, given that they were promised two gardens, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. It has also been read (qurita) as "dāniyatun" in the nominative, as the predicate (khabar) of "its shades" (ẓilāluhā), and the sentence is in the place of a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: they will not see in it a sun or a bitter cold (zamharīr), or, while the state is that its shades are drawing near. They said its meaning is: the shades of the trees of Paradise are close to the righteous (al-abrār), a canopy over them as an increase in their bliss, on the understanding that if there were a harmful sun there, its trees would be a canopy over them; but there is no sun there, nor moon.

﴿And its clusters are made easy to reach, a making easy﴾: that is, its fruits are subjected to whoever reaches for them, and their picking is made easy. It derives from "dhull" (ease/submission), which is the opposite of difficulty (ṣuʿūba). The clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "dāniyatan", meaning: its shades draw near over them while its clusters are made easy for them. Or it is conjoined to "dāniyatan ʿalayhim ẓilāluhā" with "and its clusters made easy". And on the reading of "dāniyatun" in the nominative, it is a verbal sentence (jumla fiʿliyya) conjoined to a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya).
(p-74) ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups﴾. The kub is a large jug without a handle or a loop. ﴿They were glass vessels﴾.

﴿Qawarira min fiḍḍah﴾ (qawārīra min fiḍḍatin): meaning, they were formed combining the clarity and transparency of glass with the smoothness and whiteness of silver. The phrase is a description (ṣifah) of the cups (al-akwāb). The second *qawārīra* is also read with tanwin, and both are read without tanwin. The second is read in the nominative (raf') as in (hiya qawārīru), "they are crystal vessels."

﴿Qaddarūhā taqdīrā﴾: this is a description of *qawārīra*. The meaning of their measuring them is that they determined them in their own minds, wanting them to be of specific measures and shapes that suited their desires, so they came out as they had determined. Or they measured them by their righteous deeds, so they came out in accordance with those deeds. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to those who go around serving them (al-ṭā'ifīna biha), who are indicated by the Exalted's words ﴿wa yuṭāfu 'alayhim﴾ ("and there will be circulated among them"). The meaning then is that they measured its drink according to the measure of their desire. It is also read *quddirūhā* in the passive voice (al-bināʾ lil-mafʿūl), meaning: they were made capable of it as they wished, from *qadara*, taken as transitive from *qaddartu al-shay'* ("I measured the thing").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 17:

﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾. That is: something resembling ginger in taste. And the drink mixed with it was among the most pleasant things the Arabs find pleasant and the most delicious things they take delight in.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 18:

﴿عَيْنًا﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "zanjabilan" (ginger). It has also been said that their cup is mixed with ginger of the very same spring, or that Allah Most High creates its taste within it, so that "ʿaynan" is then a substitute for "kasan" (a cup), as if it were said: "and they will be given to drink therein a cup, a cup of a spring." Or it is put in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas).

﴿فِيها تُسَمّى سَلْسَبِيلا﴾ ("therein is named Salsabil"). It is so called for the smoothness (salasa) of its descent down the throat and the ease of its passage. It is said: a drink that is salsal, salsal and salsabil. For this reason the letter ba' (ب) is judged to be an added (ziyada) letter. The purpose is to indicate that in its taste it is like ginger, yet there is no pungency (la'dh) in it; rather, the opposite of pungency is smoothness (salasa).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 19:

﴿And there will go around them youths made eternal.﴾ That is: they will remain forever in the freshness and radiance in which they are.

﴿When you see them, you would think them scattered pearls.﴾ Because of their beauty, the purity of their complexions, the brightness of their faces, their being dispersed throughout their gatherings and dwellings, and the reflection of the rays of some of them onto others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 20:

﴿And when you see there﴾ has no object, either spoken, implied, or intended. Rather, its meaning is: wherever your sight falls in Paradise.

﴿You see bliss and a great dominion﴾, that is, pleasure and vast expanse. In a hadith: "The lowest of the people of Paradise in rank is one who looks over his kingdom a distance of a thousand years, and sees its farthest part as he sees its nearest." It is also said: [the dominion] has no end. It is also said: when they desire something, it comes to be. It is also said: the angels greet them and ask permission to enter upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 21:

﴿Upon them will be garments of green fine silk﴾ (p-75). It has been said: "عالِيَهُمْ" (ʿāliyahum, "upon them") is an adverbial phrase (ẓarf, a prepositional phrase of place) functioning as a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam), and "ثِيابُ" (thiyāb, "garments") is a postponed subject (mubtada' muakhkhar, a subject placed after its predicate). The clause is another descriptive phrase (ṣifah) for "وِلْدانٌ" (wildān, "youths"), as if it were said: "Youths will circulate among them, above them are garments..." etc. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "عَلَيْهِمْ" ('alayhim, "upon them") or in "حَسِبْتَهُمْ" (ḥasibtahum, "you would think them"), meaning: youths will circulate among them, elevated over those who are being served, with garments... etc.; or: you would think them scattered pearls, elevated above them are garments... etc. It was also read as "عالِيهُمْ" (ʿāliyuhum) with a nominative ending, as a subject whose predicate is "ثِيابُ" (thiyāb), meaning: what covers them of their clothing is garments of fine silk. It was also read as "خُضْرٍ" (khuḍrin) with a genitive ending, taken as agreeing with "سُنْدُسٍ" (sundus) in meaning, since it is a noun denoting a kind (ism jins, a generic noun).

﴿and brocade﴾: "وَإسْتَبْرَقٌ" (wa-istabraq) is in the nominative, conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "ثِيابُ". It was also read with the first noun in the nominative and the second in the genitive, and vice versa, and with both in the genitive. It was read "واسْتَبْرَقَ" (wa-istabraqa) with a connecting alif and a fatḥah, as a verb form of the pattern "istaf'ala" derived from "البَرِيقُ" (al-bariq, "glitter"), and it became a proper name (ʿalam) for this type of garment.

﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾: "وَحُلُّوا" (wa-ḥullū) is conjoined to "يَطُوفُ عَلَيْهِمْ" (yaṭūfu ʿalayhim, "will circulate among them"). This is not contradicted by His saying, ﴿bracelets of gold﴾, since reconciliation is possible through combining, successive occurrence, or partial application. The adornments of the people of Paradise vary according to their deeds, so perhaps He, exalted is He, bestows upon them, as a reward for what their hands have done, adornments and lights that vary in the way gold and silver vary. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "عالِيَهُمْ", with "قَدْ" (qad) implied; on this basis it is permissible that this is for the servants and that for the ones being served.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: this is another kind that surpasses the two preceding kinds, as indicated by the attribution of its giving to the Lord of the worlds and by describing it as pure (ṭahūriyyah, purifying quality). It purifies its drinker from the defilement of inclination toward sensual pleasures and from reliance on what is other than the Truth, so that he is free to contemplate His beauty, delighted by meeting Him, abiding through His abiding. This is the furthest goal among the stations of the truthful (ṣiddīqīn), and for this reason the account of the reward of the righteous (abrār) concludes with it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 22:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ is (spoken) with an implied verb of saying, i.e., it is said to them: that this which has been mentioned of the varieties of honours,

﴿has been for you a reward﴾ in return for your good deeds, ﴿and your striving has been appreciated﴾, i.e., pleasing, accepted, and recompensed with reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Qur'an, sent down in stages.﴾ That is: in parts, gradually revealed, for profound wisdoms that necessitate this, not by any other than Us, as is expressed by the repetition of the pronoun together with "inna" (indeed).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 24:

﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord﴾, by delaying your victory over the disbelievers, for surely His outcome is a praiseworthy one.

﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾. That is: each of the one who commits sin (ithm), who calls you to it, and of the one who is extreme in disbelief (kufr), who calls you to it. The "aw" (or) indicates that the two are equal in deserving disobedience and in being independently so. The division is made with regard to what they call you to. The fact that the prohibition is attached to the two descriptors indicates that they are the cause of it. Therefore the prohibition on obeying them must be in sin and disbelief, and in what is neither sin nor disbelief. It has been said: the sinner is ʿUtba, for he was a frequent perpetrator of sins and engaged in various kinds of wickedness (fusuq), and the ungrateful one is al-Walid, for he was extreme in disbelief and severely stubborn in arrogance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 25:

﴿And mention the name of your Lord at dawn and in the evening.﴾ Persist in remembering Him at all times; or, persist in the prayers of dawn (Fajr), midday (Zuhr) and afternoon (Asr), for the evening (asil) encompasses them both.

(p-76) ﴿And of the night, prostrate yourself to Him﴾ and for part of the night, pray to Him. Perhaps this refers to the Maghrib (sunset) and 'Isha' (night) prayers. The fronting of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is because prayer in the night involves greater hardship and sincerity.

﴿And glorify Him through a long night﴾ and perform tahajjud (voluntary night prayer) for Him during long portions of the night.

Indeed, these (ﷺ no) — these disbelievers ﴿love the fleeting life﴾ and immerse themselves in its perishable pleasures.

﴿And leave behind them﴾ — i.e., before them, they make no preparation; or they cast it behind their backs (ignore it).

﴿a heavy day﴾ — which they do not heed. Describing it as heavy is a metaphor (istiʿarah) that likens its severity and terror to the weight of a crushing, burdensome thing on the one who carries it. This serves as a justification (ta'līl) for what was commanded and forbidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 28:

﴿We created them﴾, not anyone else.

﴿And We strengthened their joints﴾, meaning: We made the binding of their joints with the sinews firm.

﴿And when We will, We can replace their likes﴾ after their destruction.

﴿A replacement﴾, wondrous and beyond doubt, which is the resurrection (al-ba'th), as the word "idha" (when) indicates. Or it means "We would replace others" from among those who obey, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He could replace you with another people﴾. And "idha" (when) is for indicating the certainty of the power and the strength of the motive.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 29:

﴿Indeed, this is a reminder⁠﴾ — a reference to the surah, or to the verses nearby.

﴿So whoever wills takes a path to his Lord⁠﴾ — that is: whoever wills to take a path (sabil) to Him, exalted is He, i.e., a means (wasilah) that leads him to His reward, takes it; that is, he draws near to Him by acting upon what is contained within its verses. And the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 30:

﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ is a confirmation of the truth by showing that mere willing on their part is not sufficient for adopting the way, as is understood from the apparent meaning of the conditional clause. That is: you do not will to adopt the way, and you are not able to attain it at any time except at the time of His, exalted is He, willing its attainment for you. For the will of the servant has no role except in acquisition (kasb), while the effect and the creating belong to the will of Allah, mighty and majestic is He. It was also read: (yashā'ūn) with the ya' (i.e., "they will"), and it was read: (illā mā yashā'u Allāh) ("except what Allah wills"). His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾ is an explanation that His, exalted is He, will is founded upon knowledge and wisdom. The meaning is: He, exalted is He, is perfect in knowledge and wisdom, so He knows what each person deserves, and therefore He wills for them only what His knowledge calls for and His wisdom requires. And His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 76, verse 31:

﴿He admits whomever He wills into His mercy.﴾ This explains the rulings of His will, which follow from His knowledge and wisdom. That is, He admits into His mercy whomever He wills to admit. He is the One who directs their will toward taking the path to Him, the Exalted, by granting them success in what leads to entry into Paradise, namely faith and obedience.

﴿And the wrongdoers﴾: they are those who turned their will toward the opposite of what was mentioned. ﴿He has prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, that is, one extremely painful. Al-Zajjaj said: "The wrongdoers is in the accusative because what precedes it is in the accusative. That is: He admits whomever He wills into His mercy and punishes the wrongdoers. And 'He has prepared for them' serves as an explanation of this implied verb." It was also recited in the nominative, on the basis of inception (al-ibtida').

From the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Whoever recites the surah Hal ataa, his reward from Allah, the Exalted, will be Paradise and silk.﴾
